content.text: Reading
offsetHeight

costs almost nothing while the layout is clean, and a full layout when it isn't. After a style write, the browser has to recompute geometry before it can answer, right there inside your JavaScript. Alternate writes and reads in a loop and you pay for a layout on every pass. Read everything first, then write.

A report screen has a sticky header table and a separate body table, and a "Fit columns" button copies each header cell's width onto the cells below. With 300 rows and 6 columns, clicking it froze the page. We ran it in headless Chromium 156: the handler took between 1.9 and 3.2 s across five runs, and a trace showed 1,800 Layout events for one click. In the slowest run, the Long Animation Frames API put 3,139 ms of the handler's 3,250 ms on forced style and layout. Moving the reads out of the loop, with the same writes, brought the handler under 3 ms and down to one layout for the frame.
The common misconception
The belief: reading layout values like
offsetHeight
is free; only writing styles costs performance.
It sounds right because it's usually true. Read
offsetHeight

a hundred times in a row and nothing happens: in our trace, a hundred reads on a clean page ran zero layouts. A getter looks like a plain property access, and writes are where the visible change happens, so writes get the blame. When a profile does point at the read, it looks like a getter that happened to be slow, not like a cost your own writes created.
What actually happens
Writes are deferred, reads can't be
Setting a style doesn't make the browser recompute
layout
right away. Normally layout runs once per frame, after your JavaScript and before paint, however many styles changed. Our trace agrees: a hundred writes followed by one read ran exactly one layout.

A geometry read breaks that plan. web.dev explains that at the start of a frame, the layout values from the previous frame are known and available to query. But if your code changed styles since then, those values are stale, and the only way to answer
offsetHeight
correctly is to run style and layout now, synchronously, in the middle of your function. web.dev calls this a
forced synchronous layout
, or forced reflow, and Chrome's DevTools defines it as JavaScript querying geometric properties such as
offsetWidth
after styles were invalidated.
Which reads force it
We checked several reads, each placed right after a style write, in a loop of 100.
offsetHeight
offsetWidth
clientWidth
scrollHeight
getBoundingClientRect()
and
getComputedStyle(el).width
each forced a layout on every pass.
getComputedStyle(el).color
forced style recalculations but no layouts, since a color doesn't depend on geometry. Reading
el.style.width
or
el.className
forced neither: they return what you set, not what was computed.
Thrashing: one layout per loop iteration
One forced layout is often harmless.
Layout thrashing

is doing it repeatedly: write, read, write, read, so that every read finds the layout invalidated again. In the header table, each iteration wrote a cell width and the next iteration read a header's width, so almost every one of the 1,800 reads forced a fresh layout.

Each of those layouts is a real one. web.dev notes that layout is almost always scoped to the entire document, and that its cost grows with the size of the DOM. In our trace, the report's forced layouts took about a millisecond each: harmless once, painful 1,800 times inside a single task.
Why it shows up as slow clicks
All of this runs on the
main thread

, inside your event handler, so the browser can't paint or respond to the next input until the loop ends. web.dev ties it directly to responsiveness: to keep INP low, avoid layout when possible. Our three-second click is exactly what a user would feel as a frozen button.

content.text: To catch it on real users' devices, the Long Animation Frames API reports frames whose rendering was delayed beyond 50 ms, and each script in them carries a
forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration
. Chrome supports it from version 123; MDN still marks it experimental. This observer flagged our handler,
BUTTON#b.onclick
, and stayed silent for the fixed version:

blocks.title: Look where the Layout sits in the flame chart

content.text: In a Performance panel recording, normal layout runs after your script, in the frame's rendering work. A forced layout appears nested under your own function call. In our trace of the slow version, 1,799 of the 1,800 Layout events sat inside the click handler; in the fixed version, the single layout came after it.

blocks.title: The read can hide in a helper

content.text: Thrashing rarely looks like the textbook loop. The read sits in a
getWidth()

helper, a component's measure step or a library's position calculation, and the write in the caller. Profilers blame whichever line does the read, so the fix often means moving reads up a level, not rewriting the getter.
How to apply it in your project
Use the Performance panel in DevTools and check the Forced reflow insight. Chrome's guidance is to have no forced reflow longer than 30 ms; follow it to the function that reads.
Restructure the code into a measure phase that collects every value it needs, then a mutate phase that only writes. In loops, hoist reads out of the loop when the value doesn't change.
If you just set a width, reuse the number instead of reading it back. For sizes that change on resize, compute them once per resize, not once per element.
Send
forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration
from long animation frames to your monitoring, so regressions show up as data, not as user complaints.
Key takeaways

items.text: Style writes are deferred and cheap; a geometry read after a write forces style and layout to run immediately.
